periods.analysis: Berth & Terminal Utilization closed 2024-Q3 at 81.8%, with no prior quarter in this series for quarter-over-quarter movement, placing us just above the <=80 target and in yellow. My read is that the gateway is busy in the right ways, but the margin is thin: Crane Windows 4 and 5 at South Cargo and the Friday/Saturday cruise turnarounds are carrying more of the load than the portwide average suggests. Harborview’s seaport can absorb growth, but yellow means we manage the choreography before it becomes congestion. The watch item is simultaneous container dwell above 3.2 days and cruise provisioning on Berths C-2 through C-4 during peak weekends.
periods.recommendations: Hold the weekly berth-allocation huddle with pilots, terminal operators, and Harborview Line Services, and add a 30-day exception log for every vessel shifted more than four hours. Rebalance two discretionary RoRo calls from South Cargo to North Finger where draft and labor windows allow, and test extended gate hours on Route 17 truck access for the last two Fridays of the quarter. Keep utilization below 84% on peak operating days as the near-term control point while we work back toward the <=80 target.

periods.analysis: Utilization rose to 84.6% in 2024-Q4, up 2.8 points from 81.8%, and remains yellow. That increase is not a surprise in holiday import season and winter cruise build-up, but it does tell us the Q3 cushion was not durable. We saw tight berth sequencing at Berths 6, 7, and 8 when two delayed feeder vessels arrived inside the same tide window as the Emerald Coast cruise rotation. This is a watchful result: strong demand is welcome, but the system is leaning too hard on perfect vessel timing.
periods.recommendations: Lock a holiday-season playbook by mid-November: pre-clear reefer plugs, publish 72-hour berth forecasts, and reserve Berth 5 as the first overflow option for late-arriving feeder vessels. Direct Port Operations to review all Q4 delays over six hours with Harborview Pilots and Seaside Terminal Group, then adjust the Q1 berth matrix before the first full cruise weekend. Maintain the temporary extended gate on Thursdays and Fridays until utilization is consistently trending back toward 80%.

periods.analysis: Utilization was 84.8% in 2025-Q1, up 0.2 points from 84.6%, essentially flat but still yellow. The good news is that the Q4 jump did not accelerate; the concern is that we have now normalized operations in the mid-80s instead of near the <=80 target. Cruise passenger peaks, citrus exports, and late Asia service arrivals kept the East Basin tight even after the revised berth matrix went live. I am watching Berth 9 maintenance outages and yard dwell at Terminal B, because either one can turn a stable yellow into a service problem quickly.
periods.recommendations: Keep the revised berth matrix in place, but add a hard trigger: if projected daily utilization exceeds 87%, the duty harbor master must activate the overflow plan by 0600. Move Berth 9 maintenance into two night windows where safety permits, and require the contractor, Gulf Marine Electric, to submit a daily completion board during the outage. Start a 10-vessel pilot with appointment-based truck pickups at Terminal B to pull dwell below the pinch-point threshold.

periods.analysis: Utilization improved to 81.2% in 2025-Q2, down 3.6 points from 84.8%, the first meaningful move back toward target while still yellow. This is what disciplined operations look like: not a victory lap, but proof that the berth matrix, extended gates, and maintenance sequencing are working. The shoulder-season cruise drop helped, and so did moving two breakbulk calls to the North Finger apron after Yard Segment NF-3 was restriped. The watch item is that 81.2% leaves only 1.2 points above the <=80 target, so one storm delay or crane outage can erase the gain.
periods.recommendations: Preserve the Q2 operating pattern through the summer by keeping North Finger available for breakbulk and RoRo overflow, not just as an emergency relief valve. Expand appointment-based pickups from the 10-vessel pilot to all Terminal B calls handled by Seaside Terminal Group, with a weekly dwell report to Port Operations. Use the quieter cruise calendar to finish fender inspections on Berths C-2 and C-3 before Q4 demand returns.

periods.analysis: Utilization moved back up to 82.9% in 2025-Q3, a 1.7-point increase from 81.2%, so the measure remains yellow. The rebound is manageable, but it confirms that Q2’s improvement was partly seasonal and partly operational; we cannot count on either by itself. Summer produce imports, two weather-diverted calls from the south coast, and a crane outage on STS-04 compressed the South Cargo schedule over three separate weeks. The key watch item is resilience: when one asset is down, the berth plan must bend without pushing the whole gateway toward the high-yellow range.
periods.recommendations: Complete the STS-04 reliability review and require Harborview CraneWorks to stock the hoist-control module locally before the next peak period. Pre-authorize weather-diversion protocols with Customs, pilots, and terminal operators so diverted vessels are assigned within two hours, not negotiated call by call. Keep the North Finger overflow lane active through September weekends and publish a utilization heat map for Berths 6 through 9 every Monday.

periods.analysis: Utilization increased again to 84.2% in 2025-Q4, up 1.3 points from 82.9%, keeping us yellow and closer to the upper end of our comfort band. Holiday cargo and the full winter cruise schedule arrived together, and the port handled them, but with less slack than I want for a gateway of Harborview’s importance. Berth C-4 provisioning ran cleanly after the fender work, yet container call stacking at Berths 7 and 8 created several narrow sailing windows. The watch item is the same one I would put on the wall in the operations room: do not let high utilization masquerade as high performance if schedule reliability starts slipping.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a Q4 peak desk from 0500 to 1900 daily with Port Operations, Harborview Pilots, terminal dispatch, and cruise provisioning leads in the same decision loop. Cap nonessential berth maintenance during the final three weeks of December and shift inspections to documented night windows. Negotiate two additional off-peak labor gangs with Seaside Terminal Group for Saturdays when forecast utilization exceeds 85%.

periods.analysis: Utilization eased to 83.2% in 2026-Q1, down 1.0 point from 84.2%, a helpful move but still yellow. The peak desk reduced handoff friction, and the Saturday labor gangs gave us more room to recover from late arrivals without cascading delays. We still saw pressure around cruise turnarounds on Berths C-2 through C-4 and container stacking when airport-seaport logistics customers pushed time-sensitive cargo after Lunar New Year sailings. The direction is better, but the watch item remains schedule reliability on days when cruise, container, and fuel barge movements overlap.
periods.recommendations: Keep the peak desk as a permanent seasonal tool for Q1 and Q4, then scale it down to a weekly readiness call in shoulder quarters. Build a shared conflict calendar for cruise provisioning, fuel barge moves, and container arrivals, with Port Operations owning final tie-up priority 96 hours out. Use the 1.0-point improvement as evidence to continue the Saturday labor agreement, but tie renewal to documented reductions in vessel wait time.

periods.analysis: Utilization returned to 81.2% in 2026-Q2, down 2.0 points from 83.2%, matching the 2025-Q2 level and staying yellow just above target. This is the best position we have had since the baseline quarter, and it shows that the operational controls are becoming repeatable rather than heroic. Shoulder-season demand helped again, but the bigger story is cleaner sequencing: the conflict calendar avoided cruise-container-fuel overlaps on five high-risk days, and Terminal B appointments kept trucks off Eller Drive during the morning peak. We are close to green, but close is not the same as compliant with the <=80 target.
periods.recommendations: Convert the conflict calendar and appointment system into standard operating procedure before the next Q3 weather season, with named owners for each berth cluster. Set a summer stretch goal of two consecutive months at or below 80% by preserving overflow capacity at North Finger and limiting discretionary same-day berth changes. Prepare a capital-light options memo on yard striping, mobile gangway placement, and tug scheduling so we have ready levers if utilization starts climbing again.

periods.analysis: Berth and terminal utilization increased from 81.2% to 83.4%, moving farther above the 80% ceiling as gateway traffic grew. Growth is welcome, but this is not an on-target capacity result.
periods.recommendations: Protect overflow capacity and use the berth conflict calendar to separate cruise, cargo and fuel moves; review whether appointment changes bring utilization back toward 80%.
